# Mock Exam: QM Intermediate {#intermediate-mock-exam}









This mock exam covers all six lectures of the course. It has **100
points**, so your test score is

$$
\text{test score} = \frac{\text{points earned}}{10},
$$

on a scale from 1.00 to 10.00, with two decimals. A score below 1.00 counts
as 1.00. The lecturer enters this test score in Osiris. Osiris then rounds it to a
whole or half grade for your final course grade. A score from 5.50 to 5.74
becomes 6.0, and a score from 5.25 to 5.49 becomes 5.0. For example, 72
points give a test score of 7.20 and a final grade of 7.0. You pass with a
final grade of 6.0 or higher, that is, with 55 points or more.

You take the Intermediate exam in TestVision. It lasts 120 minutes. You may
use RStudio, Excel, the calculator in TestVision, a simple pocket
calculator, and scrap paper. The practice
exam in TestVision appears in your own TestVision account once the
lecturer publishes it. You log in with your university account. There is no separate
link. General information about TestVision for students is on the
[university page about TestVision](https://www.tilburguniversity.edu/students/studying/exams/e-assessment/testvision).

You receive the [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](code-sheet.qmd) at
the exam. Keep it open while you work on this mock exam.

Use **120 minutes** as the practice time limit, as in the exam.

## How this mock exam works

You work as in the real exam. You download a data file, you run R yourself,
and you type your answers.

All parts are open questions. You type a number with your calculation, or
one to three sentences. An answer without a calculation or an explanation
gets no points, unless the part asks only to report or to state something.

You do not have to simulate data, and you do not have to reproduce a
simulation. The practice data are invented. The code that made them is in a
collapsed box at the end of this page. It is there only so that anyone can
check how we made the data. It is not part of the exam.

A part that starts with "In R:" needs code that you write and run yourself.
Its answer is not printed in the question. For these parts, type the R
command that you used and the numbers that the part asks for. You can
answer all other parts from your own results, from printed output, or with a
short calculation. You may use R as a calculator everywhere.

Question 3 shows an R output of a colleague, and Question 4 shows a
regression table in the layout of a research paper. You interpret them.
Question 6 shows an answer of an AI assistant. You assess it.

All tests are two-sided. Use a 5% significance level. Some parts that build
on an "In R:" part print stand-in values. Use them if your code does not run.

## Dataset used throughout

The practice data are invented. Treat them as a simple random sample of 320
young ventures from a business registry. One row is one venture. The data
are observational: none of the predictors was assigned by chance.

- `growth_pct`: growth of annual sales compared with the year before, in
  percent. A value of 12 means that sales were 12% higher than in the year
  before
- `marketing_10k`: annual marketing spending, in €10,000s. The values run
  from 0.25 (€2,500) to 7.99 (€79,900)
- `experience_years`: prior industry experience of the lead founder, in
  years, from 0 to 18
- `team_size`: number of current team members, from 1 to 10
- `digital`: `No` for a mainly physical offering and `Yes` for a mainly
  digital offering. `No` is the reference category
- `spend_c`: `marketing_10k - 4`, marketing spending centred at €40,000.
  This is close to the sample mean of about €40,400.

The population is the set of ventures in this registry. The data do not
measure later survival or market conditions.

[Download `qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv`](../data/qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv),
save it in the folder `data` of your R project, and load it with the code
below. If you save the file directly in your project folder, write
`"qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv"` as the file name.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ventures <- read.csv("data/qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv")
ventures$digital <- factor(ventures$digital, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
```
:::




## Question 1: Simple regression (13 points)

A founder asks whether ventures that spend more on marketing grow faster.
The outcome is `growth_pct` and the predictor is `marketing_10k`.

1. In R: load the data and check that the file has 320 rows. Report the
   mean and the largest value of `growth_pct`. **(2 points: 1 + 1)**
2. In R: fit the simple regression of `growth_pct` on `marketing_10k`.
   Report the intercept and the slope. **(2 points: 1 + 1)**

   Stand-in values, if your code does not run: intercept 6.6 and slope 1.4.
   Use them in parts 3 and 4.
3. Interpret the slope in one sentence. **(4 points)**
4. In R: use `predict()` to calculate the fitted growth of a venture that
   spends €50,000 on marketing. The actual sales growth of this venture is 11%.
   Calculate its residual. State what the sign of the residual means.
   **(5 points: 3 + 1 + 1)**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

1. The mean sales growth is 12.172% (1 point). The largest sales growth is
   31.940% (1 point). Both numbers are in the output of `summary(ventures)`.
2. Intercept 6.598 and slope 1.378 (1 point each, within 0.001). The fitted
   line is $\widehat{growth\_pct}=6.598+1.378\,marketing\_10k$. The stand-in
   values 6.6 and 1.4 earn no points here.
3. Among the 320 sampled ventures, a venture that spends €10,000 more on
   marketing has on average 1.38 percentage points higher fitted sales
   growth. One point each for: the size and direction (1.38 higher), the
   step of the predictor (€10,000 more marketing spending), the unit of the
   outcome (percentage points of sales growth), and the wording as an
   association. An answer with "causes", "leads to", or "will raise" loses
   the last point. With the stand-in value the size is 1.4.
4. €50,000 is `marketing_10k = 5`. The command
   `predict(simple_model, newdata = data.frame(marketing_10k = 5))` gives a
   fitted growth of 13.490% (3 points: 1 for the value 5, 2 for the fitted
   growth). The calculation by hand,
   $6.598+1.378\times5=13.49$%, also earns the 2 points. The residual is
   $11-13.49=-2.49$ percentage points (1 point). The sign is negative: this
   venture grew less than the fitted growth for ventures with the same
   marketing spending (1 point). With the stand-in values the fitted growth is
   $6.6+1.4\times5=13.60$% and the residual is $-2.60$ percentage points.
   These earn all 5 points.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
new_venture <- data.frame(marketing_10k = 5)
fit_50k <- unname(predict(simple_model, newdata = new_venture))
c(fitted = fit_50k, residual = 11 - fit_50k)
```

## Question 2: Assumptions and diagnostics (15 points)

Check the model of Question 1, `growth_pct ~ marketing_10k`. Parts 1 and 4
ask for two plots. If your plots do not work, open the stand-in figure
below part 4 and answer from it.

1. In R: make the residual-versus-fitted plot of the model. Describe in one
   sentence the pattern that you see. State the assumption that this pattern
   challenges. **(5 points: 3 + 2)**
2. In R: count the ventures with a standardised residual beyond $\pm3$.
   Then count the ventures with a Cook's distance above $4/n$. Report both
   counts. **(2 points: 1 + 1)**
3. A colleague wants to delete all ventures that part 2 flags, "to get a
   cleaner model". Respond to her plan in two or three sentences. State the
   rule of Lecture 2 for flagged observations, and say what you would do
   with these ventures. **(4 points: 1 + 3)**
4. In R: make the normal Q--Q plot of the standardised residuals. Describe
   in one sentence how the points lie relative to the line. Then explain in
   one sentence whether a departure from normality is a serious problem for
   this model with 320 ventures. **(4 points: 1 + 3)**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Stand-in figure for parts 1 and 4 (open it only if your own plots do not work)




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"}
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
simple_model <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k, data = ventures)

resid_df <- data.frame(
  fitted = fitted(simple_model),
  residual = residuals(simple_model)
)
qq_df <- data.frame(rs = rstandard(simple_model))
theme_mock <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )

p_resid <- ggplot(resid_df, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#C98B2E",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6, colour = "#009E73") +
  labs(x = "Fitted growth (%)",
       y = "Residual (percentage points)") +
  theme_mock

p_qq <- ggplot(qq_df, aes(sample = rs)) +
  geom_qq_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_qq(colour = "#009E73", alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  labs(x = "Normal theoretical quantile",
       y = "Standardised residual") +
  theme_mock

p_resid + p_qq
```

The dashed line in the left panel marks a residual of zero.](mock-exam_files/figure-html/fig-imock-diagnostics-1.png){#fig-imock-diagnostics width=672}

## Model answer and marking guide

The two plots with the commands of the code sheet:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
simple_model <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k, data = ventures)
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.4, 1.3, 0.7), las = 1)
plot(fitted(simple_model), residuals(simple_model),
     xlab = "Fitted growth (%)", ylab = "Residual (percentage points)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(rstandard(simple_model), main = "",
       xlab = "Normal theoretical quantile",
       ylab = "Standardised residual")
qqline(rstandard(simple_model))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](mock-exam_files/figure-html/imock-q2-plots-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(old_par)
```
:::




1. The vertical spread of the residuals grows from left to right, that is,
   with the fitted growth. The points form a fan (3 points). Give 1 point
   for "the spread changes" and 3 points for "the spread grows with the
   fitted growth" or "a fan". This challenges the assumption of constant
   variance of the errors (2 points, also for "homoskedasticity"). The
   assumption earns 2 points or none. No clear curve is visible in this
   plot. An answer that names only "linearity" earns no points for the
   assumption. An answer that names constant variance and also mentions a
   slight curve keeps the 2 points. The code below confirms what you see in
   the plot.
   The standard deviation of the residuals is 3.40 percentage points in the
   third of the ventures with the lowest fitted growth and 5.42 in the third
   with the highest.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
thirds <- cut(
  fitted(simple_model),
  breaks = quantile(fitted(simple_model), c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)),
  include.lowest = TRUE, labels = c("lowest", "middle", "highest")
)
tapply(residuals(simple_model), thirds, sd)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  lowest   middle  highest 
3.402068 4.652011 5.421291 
```


:::
:::




2. One venture has a standardised residual beyond $\pm3$ (1 point). 19
   ventures have a Cook's distance above $4/n=4/320=0.0125$ (1 point).




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(abs(rstandard(simple_model)) > 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(cooks.distance(simple_model) > 4 / nobs(simple_model))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 19
```


:::
:::




3. The rule is: investigate, report, never silently delete (1 point).
   Investigate means to look at the flagged ventures in the data and to ask
   whether a value is an error or whether the venture is of a different kind
   (1 point). Report means to fit the model with and without these ventures
   (1 point), to show both results, and to say which one you use and why
   (1 point).
4. The points follow the line in the middle. At the upper end they lie
   above the line, and near the lower end slightly below it (1 point for
   "close to the line in the middle, away from it at the ends"). This is not
   a serious problem here. Normal errors matter in small samples. With 320
   ventures the tests and intervals still hold approximately (3 points: 1
   for the decision, 1 for "normal errors matter in small samples", 1 for
   the sample size of 320). The fan of part 1 is the bigger problem.
:::

## Question 3: Inference and fit (10 points)

A colleague drew 200 of the 320 ventures at random and fitted the model
below to these 200 ventures. You do not know which ventures she drew, so you
cannot run this model yourself. Answer from her output. The formulas are on
the code sheet.

```text
Call:
lm(formula = growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + experience_years + 
    digital, data = ventures_200)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-11.2970  -2.7338  -0.0992   2.6132  12.3786 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       2.73159    0.78897   3.462 0.000658 ***
marketing_10k     1.35473    0.12868  10.528  < 2e-16 ***
experience_years  0.28585    0.05277   5.417 1.77e-07 ***
digitalYes        3.17544    0.58246   5.452 1.49e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.049 on 196 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4803,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.4723 
F-statistic: 60.38 on 3 and 196 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
```

For this model, SSE = 3212.85 and SST = 6181.93. The critical value for a
95% confidence interval and a 5% test with 196 degrees of freedom is
$t_{0.975,\,196}=1.972$. In R, `qt(0.975, 196)` gives it.

1. (a) Show with a calculation how the Multiple R-squared follows from SSE
   and SST. (b) State in one sentence what this number says about the model
   for these 200 ventures. **(4 points: 2 + 2)**
2. (a) Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the coefficient of
   `marketing_10k`. Write the five parts of the
   [exam procedure of Lecture 3](i03-inference-fit-ftest.qmd#i03-exam-procedure). (b)
   State whether the 5% test rejects a coefficient of zero, and explain how the
   interval shows this. **(6 points: 4 + 2)**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Model answer and marking guide

The code below is the code of the colleague. We show it so that you can
check every printed number.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
rows_200 <- sort(sample(nrow(ventures), 200))
ventures_200 <- ventures[rows_200, ]
model_200 <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + experience_years + digital,
  data = ventures_200
)
summary(model_200)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

    digital, data = ventures_200)

Residuals:

-11.2970  -2.7338  -0.0992   2.6132  12.3786 

Coefficients:

(Intercept)       2.73159    0.78897   3.462 0.000658 ***
marketing_10k     1.35473    0.12868  10.528  < 2e-16 ***
experience_years  0.28585    0.05277   5.417 1.77e-07 ***
```

```{.r .cell-code}
SSE_200 <- sum(residuals(model_200)^2)
SST_200 <- sum((ventures_200$growth_pct - mean(ventures_200$growth_pct))^2)
c(SSE = SSE_200, SST = SST_200, R2 = 1 - SSE_200 / SST_200)
```

1. (a) $R^2=1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}=1-3212.85/6181.93$ (1 point) $=0.48$
   (1 point). (b) Among these 200 ventures, the model explains about 48% of
   the variation in sales growth (2 points: 1 for "share of the variation of
   the outcome that the model explains", 1 for naming the outcome and the
   sample). "48% of the predictions are correct" earns no points for (b).
2. (a) The five parts of the interval:
   1. **Formula.** $\hat\beta_j\pm t_{0.975,\,df}\,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)$,
      with $df=n-k-1=200-3-1=196$.
   2. **Given values.** $\hat\beta_j=1.35473$,
      $\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)=0.12868$, and
      $t_{0.975,\,196}=1.972$.
   3. **Calculations.** The margin of error is $1.972\times0.12868=0.254$.
   4. **Interval.** $(1.355-0.254,\ 1.355+0.254)=(1.10,\ 1.61)$ percentage
      points per €10,000.
   5. **Conclusion.** See (b).

   Marking of (a): 1 point for the formula with the given values, 1 for the
   margin of error 0.254, 1 for both ends, and 1 for the unit. (b) Zero lies
   outside the interval (1 point). The interval contains the values of the
   coefficient that the two-sided 5% test does not reject, so the test
   rejects a coefficient of zero. At the 5% level we can conclude the
   following for all ventures in the registry: at the same experience and
   offering type, more marketing spending goes with higher sales growth
   (1 point).
:::

## Question 4: Multiple regression and a dummy predictor (23 points)

The table below has the layout of a regression table in a research paper.
It shows three models of sales growth (`growth_pct`), fitted to all 320
ventures of the practice data. You do not need to run these models for
parts 1 to 3.

::: {.reg-table}

|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Marketing spending (€10,000s) | 1.340\*\*\* | 1.338\*\*\* | 1.341\*\*\* |
| | (0.106) | (0.100) | (0.100) |
| Digital offering (1 = yes) | 2.969\*\*\* | 3.016\*\*\* | 3.084\*\*\* |
| | (0.488) | (0.462) | (0.463) |

Outcome: sales growth (%). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in
parentheses. All three columns use the same 320 ventures. The reference
group of the dummy is ventures with a mainly physical offering.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.

The critical value for a 95% confidence interval and a 5% test is
$t_{0.975,\,df}=1.967$ in all three columns. For column (3), with
$df=320-4-1=315$, R gives it with `qt(0.975, 315)`.

1. Team size has no star in column (3). Calculate its t value. Then state
   what the missing star means and what it does not mean.
   **(4 points: 1 + 2 + 1)**
2. Venture B spends €30,000 more on marketing than venture A. Its lead
   founder has 4 more years of experience. B has a digital offering and A a
   physical one. Both have the same team size. Calculate the fitted growth
   of B minus the fitted growth of A with column (3). **(5 points)**
3. Founder experience has three stars in column (2). Still, adding it moves
   the marketing coefficient only from 1.340 to 1.338. Explain in one or two
   sentences what this says about experience and marketing spending in this
   sample. Then state one problem that the stable coefficient does not
   exclude. **(5 points: 3 + 2)**
4. In R: test whether founder experience and team size together improve the
   model of column (1). Fit the models of columns (1) and (3) and compare
   them with `anova()`. Report the F statistic. Then show how F follows from
   the two residual sums of squares in your output.
   **(4 points: 1 + 3)**

   Stand-in values, if your code does not run: the residual sum of squares
   is about 5950 on 317 degrees of freedom for column (1). It is about
   5270 on 315 degrees of freedom for column (3). Calculate F from them.
   For part 5, use a p-value below 0.001.
5. State the null hypothesis of the test in part 4 and your conclusion at
   the 5% level. Then explain in one sentence how this conclusion and the
   missing star of team size can both be true. **(5 points: 1 + 2 + 2)**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

Sara runs a young venture with a mainly digital offering. She gave column

She asked: "What does this mean for my marketing budget?" The AI answered:

Sara's venture had sales of €1,000,000 last year. So 1 percentage point of

## Model answer and marking guide

The calculation $2\times1.341=2.68$ in the AI answer is correct. The
wording around it is not.

1. (a) No. A control holds fixed only what is measured and in the model
   (1 point). Variables that are not in the data can influence both marketing
   spending and growth (1 point), for example the quality of the product
   (1 point for one concrete variable that is not in the model). (b) "At
   the same experience, team size, and offering type, ventures that spend
   €20,000 more on marketing have on average 2.68 percentage points higher
   fitted sales growth." Give 1 point for 2.68 percentage points with the
   step of €20,000, and 1 point for a comparison of ventures at the same
   experience, team size, and offering type. A sentence with "will rise" or
   "causes" loses the second point.
2. Two of the three errors, 1 point each. The outcome is in percent, so
   the difference is 3.084 percentage points, not 3.084%: "3.084% faster"
   would be a relative change. The comparison is with the reference group,
   ventures with a mainly physical offering, and not with the average
   venture. The AI sentence also does not say what is held fixed. A correct
   sentence (2 points: 1 for percentage points and the physical reference
   group, 1 for what is held fixed): "Ventures with a mainly digital
   offering have on average 3.084 percentage points higher fitted sales
   growth than ventures with a mainly physical offering that have the same
   marketing spending, experience, and team size."
3. (a) No. A p-value is calculated under the assumptions of the model
   (1 point), so it cannot prove them (1 point). (b) The small p-value is
   evidence against a marketing coefficient of zero (1 point), if the
   assumptions hold (1 point).

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(734)
n_mock <- 320
marketing_10k <- round(runif(n_mock, 0.25, 8), 2)
experience_years <- sample(0:18, n_mock, replace = TRUE)
team_size <- sample(
  1:10, n_mock, replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(8, 16, 20, 20, 14, 9, 6, 4, 2, 1)
)
digital <- factor(
  ifelse(runif(n_mock) < 0.45, "Yes", "No"),
  levels = c("No", "Yes")
)
spend_c <- marketing_10k - 4
growth_mean <-
  8 + 1.10 * spend_c + 3 * (digital == "Yes") -
  0.10 * spend_c^2 + 0.30 * experience_years +
  0.70 * spend_c * (digital == "Yes") + 0.20 * team_size
growth_pct <- round(
  growth_mean + rnorm(n_mock, 0, 2.5 + 0.40 * marketing_10k),
  2
)
ventures <- data.frame(
  growth_pct, marketing_10k, experience_years, team_size, digital, spend_c
)
```
